issues.legal_issue: A refusal to grant leave to appeal against an acquittal must state reasons sufficient to show that the court applied its mind.
material_facts: The State sought leave to appeal against an acquittal.

The trial court had considered an admission of encroachment, official witness testimony and documentary evidence, but acquitted the accused on grounds concerning proof of notification and compliance with prescribed procedures.
The High Court refused leave in a one-line order without giving reasons.
The Supreme Court considered the evidentiary and legal questions substantial enough to require adjudication in an appeal.
issues.conclusion: The unreasoned refusal was unsustainable and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court considering leave to appeal against an acquittal must give reasons indicating application of mind. Reasons enable the affected party to understand the decision and allow appellate or judicial review; they are an essential feature of judicial decision-making. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Battan, State of Maharashtra v. Vithal Rao Pritirao Chawan, Jawahar Lal Singh v. Naresh Singh, Raj Kishore Jha v. State of Bihar and State of Punjab v. Bhag Singh, and referred to the duty to follow this Court’s declarations under Article 141 of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.leave_sought: The appellant asks the High Court for leave to appeal against the acquittal.
predicates.refusal_without_reasons: The High Court refuses leave without stating reasons that indicate application of its mind.

issues.definition: If leave is sought in an appeal against an acquittal and the refusal gives no reasons, the refusal is unsustainable.

issues.legal_issue: Leave to appeal against an acquittal should be granted when the trial court has failed to carefully appraise material evidence requiring appellate examination.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding that the admission of encroachment was insufficient and that proof of notification and compliance with prescribed procedures was lacking.
The prosecution had also presented testimony from official witnesses and a sketch map of the occupied land.
The Supreme Court considered the effect of the admission in the context of the testimony and documents to require adjudication in an appeal.
The Supreme Court found that the trial court had not performed its duty to carefully appraise the evidence and that the High Court had not undertaken appellate examination.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought to have granted leave and then independently reappraised the evidence as the first appellate court; the matter was remitted for the appeal to be heard and decided according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 378(1) and 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, where the trial court has failed to carefully appraise the evidence, the High Court should grant leave and, as the first court of appeal, independently reappraise the record and determine guilt or innocence objectively.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and leave_sought and trial_court_failed_to_appraise_evidence and material_evidence_requires_appellate_examination

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.leave_sought: The appellant asks the High Court for leave to appeal against the acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_failed_to_appraise_evidence: The trial court did not carefully assess the evidence before reaching its conclusion.
predicates.material_evidence_requires_appellate_exa: Evidence material to the decision requires examination by the appellate court.

issues.definition: When leave is sought in an appeal against an acquittal, the trial court failed to appraise the evidence, and material evidence requires appellate examination, leave should be granted for independent appellate review.
